title: Grade 8
emphasis: Nuance, tone, and stronger academic language

words.definition: showing great, careful attention to every small detail

hero.text: Pixel was meticulous when rewiring the academy's alarm panel, labeling every wire and testing each connection twice.

words.everyday: The museum conservator was meticulous, cleaning the old painting one square centimeter at a time with a tiny brush.

contrast.nonExample: Theo copied his lab data quickly, skipped two measurements, and guessed the rest.
contrast.explanation: Meticulous work checks every detail with care. Rushing and guessing is careless, the opposite of meticulous.

items.prompt: Which student is being meticulous?

options.text: Ines finishes her map first and hands it in without looking it over.
Omar measures each border twice and checks every label against the atlas.
Lucy decorates her map with bright colors and stickers.
Dev asks a friend to finish his map for him.

items.hint: Meticulous is about care with small details. Who checks everything?
items.explanation: Meticulous means paying careful attention to every detail. Omar measures twice and checks each label, which is meticulous.

wrong.a: Ines is fast, not careful; she never checks her work.
wrong.c: Decorating is creative, but it doesn't show attention to accuracy.
wrong.d: Handing off the work shows no care at all.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The archaeologists were ___ as they uncovered the ancient pottery. They brushed away soil grain by grain and photographed every shard before moving it.
items.clue: grain by grain; photographed every shard
items.hint: Look at how slowly and carefully the team works.
items.explanation: "Grain by grain" and "photographed every shard" show extreme care with details, so meticulous fits. Reckless and impatient describe the opposite kind of work.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the writer's admiring tone?
items.passage: Thanks to Mrs. Okafor's ___ records, the historical society could trace every family that had lived on Elm Street since 1890.
items.clue: Thanks to; could trace every family
items.hint: Fussy and nitpicky both involve detail. Which one sounds like praise?
items.explanation: Meticulous means careful with detail in a positive, admiring way. Fussy and nitpicky also involve detail but suggest the care is annoying or excessive. "Thanks to" shows the writer is praising her.

wrong.a: Fussy has a negative tone: worrying too much about small things.
wrong.c: Nitpicky is critical, not admiring.
wrong.d: Messy records couldn't trace every family.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what meticulous means.

chunks.text: The meticulous editor
read the article three times
and corrected every misplaced comma.
and skimmed it while chatting on the phone.

items.hint: A meticulous person notices even tiny mistakes.
items.explanation: Rereading three times and fixing every comma shows meticulous attention to detail. Skimming while distracted is careless.

wrong.c4: Skimming while chatting shows a lack of care, not meticulous work.

items.prompt: Is this an example of being meticulous?
items.passage: Before the orchestra concert, Rosa tuned her violin, then tuned it again after the stage lights warmed the room, and marked every tricky bowing in her music with a pencil.
items.hint: Does Rosa pay close attention to small details?
items.explanation: Retuning after the room warms and marking every tricky bowing are small details most people would skip. That careful attention is meticulous.

words.definition: certain to happen; impossible to avoid or prevent

hero.text: Kai knew the storm's arrival was inevitable, so instead of trying to stop it, he helped the town prepare.

words.everyday: Once the glacier's ice began melting faster than snow could replace it, its shrinking was inevitable.

contrast.nonExample: The team might win the game if their best player recovers in time.
contrast.explanation: Something that might or might not happen is uncertain. Inevitable means it is sure to happen no matter what.

items.prompt: What does "inevitable" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: If you drop an ice cube on a hot sidewalk, its melting is inevitable.
items.hint: Can anything stop ice from melting on a hot sidewalk?
items.explanation: Ice on a hot sidewalk will melt no matter what, so inevitable means certain to happen. "Easy to stop" is the opposite.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The bridge had been ignored for decades. Its steel was rusted through and its supports were cracking, so engineers warned that collapse was ___ unless repairs began immediately.
items.clue: rusted through; cracking; unless repairs began
items.hint: With damage this bad, how sure are the engineers that it will fall?
items.explanation: Rusted steel and cracking supports mean that, without repairs, collapse can't be avoided. That is inevitable. Unlikely and harmless contradict the warning.

items.prompt: In- means "not," and -able means "able to be." The Latin root evit means "avoid." What does inevitable literally mean?
items.hint: Put the parts together: not + avoid + able to be.
items.explanation: In- (not) + evit (avoid) + -able (able to be) = not able to be avoided. That is why inevitable means certain to happen.

wrong.a: This leaves out in-, which means not.
wrong.c: The root means avoid, not see.
wrong.d: Inevitable is not related to invite, even though they look a little alike.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what inevitable means.

chunks.text: Because the river kept rising all night,
flooding in the low fields
was inevitable.
was a rare and unexpected surprise.

items.hint: If the river keeps rising, can the flooding be avoided?
items.explanation: A river rising all night makes flooding certain, so it was inevitable. A "rare and unexpected surprise" is the opposite of something certain.

wrong.c4: An unexpected surprise is not inevitable; inevitable things are expected and unavoidable.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the outcome the historian describes?
items.passage: By 1780, the colonists and the British government disagreed on almost everything, and neither side would compromise. Many historians argue that, by then, a final break between them could not have been prevented.
items.clue: could not have been prevented
items.hint: Find the phrase that tells whether the break could be stopped.
items.explanation: "Could not have been prevented" defines inevitable. Doubtful means uncertain, which contradicts the historians' view.

words.definition: to examine something very closely and critically, looking for details or flaws

hero.text: Juniper scrutinized the security footage frame by frame until she spotted the shadow by the door.

words.everyday: Before signing the lease, Ms. Patel scrutinized every line for hidden fees.

contrast.nonExample: Jordan glanced at the poster on his way to class.
contrast.explanation: A quick glance is the opposite of scrutinizing. To scrutinize, you study something slowly and critically.

items.prompt: Is this person scrutinizing something?
items.passage: Leila skimmed the headline of the news article and scrolled on to the next post.
items.hint: Scrutinizing takes slow, close attention. Did Leila do that?
items.explanation: Skimming a headline and scrolling on is quick and shallow. Scrutinizing means examining closely and critically, so this does not fit.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Before the bill became law, members of the committee ___ every section, questioning the costs and searching for loopholes.
items.clue: questioning the costs; searching for loopholes
items.hint: Questioning and searching for problems is a kind of close, critical reading.
items.explanation: "Questioning" and "searching for loopholes" show critical, detailed examination, which is scrutinizing. Memorizing involves attention but not looking for flaws.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the passage?
items.passage: The scientists did not just look at the surprising results. They ___ the data, rechecking every calculation and testing for errors before publishing.
items.clue: did not just look; rechecking every calculation
items.hint: The passage says they did more than just look. Which word is the most intense and critical?
items.explanation: Noticed, viewed, and peeked at all mean seeing, but scrutinized means examining closely and critically. "Rechecking every calculation" signals that deeper level.

wrong.a: Noticing is just becoming aware of something.
wrong.b: Viewing is looking, with no sense of critical checking.
wrong.d: Peeking is a quick look, the opposite of what the passage describes.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what scrutinize means.

chunks.text: The art expert
scrutinized the brushstrokes under a magnifier
to decide whether the painting was a forgery.
scrutinized the painting in a quick, careless glance

items.hint: Scrutinizing is slow and close, not quick.
items.explanation: Examining brushstrokes under a magnifier to judge a forgery is close, critical study, which is scrutinizing. "A quick, careless glance" contradicts the meaning.

wrong.c4: You can't scrutinize something in a quick, careless glance; the two ideas clash.

items.prompt: Which line uses "scrutinize" naturally?

options.text: "I scrutinized the movie poster for a second as I walked by."
"Let's scrutinize lunch by eating it quickly."
"The judges will scrutinize every dive, so point your toes."
"She scrutinized her nap and woke up refreshed."

items.hint: Who would examine something closely, looking for flaws?
items.explanation: Diving judges examine every detail looking for flaws, which is scrutinizing. A one-second look, eating quickly, or napping involve no close examination.

wrong.a: "For a second" is too quick to be scrutinizing.
wrong.b: Eating quickly isn't examining anything.
wrong.d: You can't examine a nap closely; the word doesn't make sense here.

words.definition: to restore friendly relations between people, or to make two ideas or facts agree

hero.text: After weeks of arguing about strategy, Rex and Bolt finally reconciled and agreed to train together again.

words.everyday: The historian tried to reconcile two diaries that described the same battle in completely different ways.

contrast.nonExample: After their argument, the two neighbors built a taller fence and stopped speaking.
contrast.explanation: Reconciling means coming back together or making things agree. Cutting off contact keeps the conflict going.

items.prompt: What does "reconciled" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: After not speaking for a year, the two brothers reconciled at their grandmother's birthday party.
items.hint: They hadn't spoken for a year. What changed at the party?
items.explanation: After a year of silence, the brothers became friendly again. Reconciled means made peace.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The witness said the car was red, but the video showed a blue car. Detectives struggled to ___ the two accounts.
items.clue: red; blue; two accounts
items.hint: The two accounts disagree. What would detectives want to do with them?
items.explanation: The witness and the video disagree, so detectives try to make them fit together, which is to reconcile them. This is the "make ideas agree" sense of reconcile.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly OPPOSITE to "reconcile" in this sentence?
items.passage: The coach hoped to reconcile the two teammates before the championship.
items.hint: Reconcile brings people together. What pushes them apart?
items.explanation: Reconcile means bringing people back into friendship; divide means pushing them apart. Reunite is a synonym, not an opposite.

wrong.a: Reunite means almost the same as reconcile.
wrong.b: Encourage isn't the opposite; it's unrelated to conflict.
wrong.c: Training is not about friendship or conflict.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what reconcile means.

chunks.text: After a long talk,
the two friends reconciled
and laughed about their silly argument.
and refused to look at each other again.

items.hint: When people reconcile, their relationship gets better.
items.explanation: Laughing together after a talk shows the friends made peace. Refusing to look at each other means they did not reconcile.

wrong.c4: Refusing to look at each other shows the conflict continued.

items.prompt: What is the scientist trying to do?
items.passage: One experiment suggested the medicine worked; another found it had no effect. Dr. Huang spent months trying to reconcile the results, eventually discovering that the two studies had used different doses.

options.text: explain how the two results could both make sense
prove that one study was dishonest
hide the results from the public

items.clue: eventually discovering that the two studies had used different doses
items.hint: What did her discovery about doses accomplish?
items.explanation: Finding that the doses differed explained why both results could be true. Reconciling results means making seemingly conflicting facts fit together.

words.definition: having to do with beauty, art, or how something looks and feels to the senses

hero.text: Nova redesigned the academy's emblem for aesthetic reasons; the old one worked fine, but it looked cluttered.

words.everyday: The architect chose curved windows for aesthetic appeal, even though square ones would have been cheaper.

contrast.nonExample: The engineers added a thicker beam so the bridge could hold heavier trucks.
contrast.explanation: That choice is about strength and function. An aesthetic choice is about beauty or appearance.

items.prompt: What does "aesthetic" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The garden designer arranged the flowers by color for aesthetic effect.
items.hint: Why would someone arrange flowers by color?
items.explanation: Arranging flowers by color is about how they look. Aesthetic means related to beauty or appearance.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The new library is energy-efficient and easy to navigate. Its ___ qualities are just as impressive: sunlight pours through stained-glass panels onto smooth wooden shelves.
items.clue: sunlight pours through stained-glass panels; smooth wooden shelves
items.hint: The second sentence describes how the building looks and feels.
items.explanation: Stained glass and smooth wood describe beauty and appearance, so aesthetic fits. "Energy-efficient" and "easy to navigate" describe practical qualities, which the passage contrasts with.

items.prompt: Is this decision made for aesthetic reasons?
items.passage: The skateboard company switched to a stronger glue because the old boards kept cracking.
items.hint: Is the change about how the boards look or how they work?
items.explanation: Stronger glue fixes cracking, which is about function and durability. An aesthetic reason would be about beauty or appearance.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what aesthetic means.

chunks.text: The photographer waited for sunset
for purely aesthetic reasons:
the golden light made the old barn glow.
the battery in her camera was running low.

items.hint: An aesthetic reason is about beauty.
items.explanation: Golden light making a barn glow is about beauty, an aesthetic reason. A low battery is a practical reason, not an aesthetic one.

wrong.c4: A low battery is a practical problem, not a reason based on beauty.

items.prompt: Which word best completes the critic's review?
items.passage: The film's plot was confusing, but its ___ achievement was undeniable: every scene looked like a carefully composed painting.
items.clue: every scene looked like a carefully composed painting
items.hint: Which word fits a formal review about artistic beauty?
items.explanation: Aesthetic names the whole area of beauty and artistic design, which suits a formal critic. Pretty and fancy are casual and describe surface looks, not an artistic achievement.

wrong.a: "Pretty achievement" sounds casual and odd in a formal review.
wrong.c: Fancy suggests showy decoration, not artistic quality.
wrong.d: Factual is about truth, not beauty.

words.definition: having mixed or conflicting feelings about something at the same time

hero.text: Bolt felt ambivalent about leading the mission: proud to be chosen, but worried about letting the team down.

words.everyday: Mara was ambivalent about moving to a new city; she was excited about the big park nearby but sad to leave her friends.

contrast.nonExample: Jamal was thrilled about the field trip and counted down the days.
contrast.explanation: Jamal has only one strong feeling. Ambivalent means feeling two opposing ways at once.

items.prompt: Which person is ambivalent?

options.text: Nico loves the new school schedule and tells everyone.
Hana is glad the season is over but already misses her teammates.
Pablo hasn't heard about the new schedule yet.
Grace is angry that practice was canceled.

items.hint: Look for someone with two opposite feelings at once.
items.explanation: Hana feels glad and sad at the same time. Ambivalent means having mixed feelings.

wrong.a: Nico has one clear feeling: happy.
wrong.c: Pablo has no opinion yet; that is not the same as mixed feelings.
wrong.d: Grace has one clear feeling: anger.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Many townspeople were ___ about the new factory. It would bring hundreds of jobs, yet it might also pollute the river they loved.
items.clue: would bring hundreds of jobs, yet it might also pollute
items.hint: "Yet" connects a good side and a bad side. How would that make people feel?
items.explanation: Jobs are good, pollution is bad, and "yet" shows people feel both. That is ambivalent. Indifferent means not caring at all, which is different from caring in two directions.

wrong.a: Enthusiastic is purely positive.
wrong.b: Furious is purely negative.
wrong.d: Indifferent means having no feelings, not mixed ones.

items.prompt: Which word best describes how Ellie feels?
items.passage: Ellie won the art contest, but her best friend, who worked just as hard, didn't place. She smiled for the photo while feeling a tug of guilt.
items.clue: smiled for the photo while feeling a tug of guilt
items.hint: She has two feelings pulling in different directions.
items.explanation: Ellie is happy to win and guilty about her friend at the same time. Ambivalent names mixed feelings. Confused means not understanding, but Ellie understands the situation clearly.

wrong.a: Indifferent means not caring; Ellie cares a lot.
wrong.b: Confused means unable to understand, which is not her problem.
wrong.d: Ellie won, so she has nothing to be jealous of.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what ambivalent means.

chunks.text: Diego felt ambivalent about the long hike:
the views would be amazing,
but his legs were already sore.
and he had no doubts at all.

items.hint: Ambivalent means feeling two ways. Show a good side and a bad side.
items.explanation: Amazing views versus sore legs shows two opposing feelings, which is ambivalent. "No doubts at all" describes certainty instead.

wrong.c4: Having no doubts is the opposite of feeling ambivalent.

items.prompt: The prefix ambi- means "both," as in ambidextrous (able to use both hands). How does this help explain ambivalent?

options.text: It means feeling strongly in both directions at once.
It means feeling nothing in either direction.
It means being able to do two jobs.
It means changing your mind every day.

items.hint: Ambi- means both. Both what, when it comes to feelings?
items.explanation: Ambi- (both) shows that an ambivalent person feels both ways at once, like wanting and not wanting something. It is not the same as feeling nothing.

wrong.b: Feeling nothing is indifference, not ambivalence.
wrong.c: Ambivalent is about feelings, not skills.
wrong.d: Ambivalence is two feelings at the same time, not switching over days.

words.definition: something that is different from what is normal, usual, or expected

hero.text: Pixel's sensors detected an anomaly: one building downtown was glowing on the heat map at midnight.

words.everyday: A snowstorm in May was an anomaly for the small desert town.

contrast.nonExample: Like every other morning, the school bus arrived at 7:45.
contrast.explanation: An event that happens as usual is normal. An anomaly breaks the usual pattern.

items.prompt: Is this an anomaly?
items.passage: In a class where students usually score between 70 and 90, one student scores a perfect 100 on every test all year.
items.hint: Does this result stand out from the usual pattern?
items.explanation: Scores usually fall between 70 and 90, so perfect scores all year are far outside the normal pattern. That makes them an anomaly.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: All twenty plants grew taller under bright light except one, which shrank. The researchers marked that plant as ___ and began looking for a cause.
items.clue: All twenty plants grew taller except one
items.hint: One plant behaved differently from all the others.
items.explanation: One plant shrank while the rest grew, so it broke the pattern. That is an anomaly. A pattern is what the other nineteen showed.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "anomaly" in this sentence?
items.passage: The astronomer noticed an anomaly in the planet's orbit, a small wobble no one could explain.
items.hint: The wobble is something unusual in an otherwise regular orbit.
items.explanation: An irregularity is something that doesn't follow the normal pattern, just like an anomaly. A mistake implies someone did something wrong, but an anomaly might be completely real.

wrong.a: An anomaly is not necessarily an error; it may be a real, unexplained difference.
wrong.b: Routine is the opposite: what normally happens.
wrong.d: Noticing it may lead to a discovery, but the anomaly itself is the oddity.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what anomaly means.

chunks.text: The 50-degree day in January
was an anomaly,
since temperatures there rarely rise above freezing in winter.
since it is that warm almost every January day.

items.hint: An anomaly is unusual. Which ending shows the day was unusual?
items.explanation: Temperatures rarely rise above freezing, so a 50-degree day breaks the pattern, making it an anomaly. If it were warm almost every day, it would be normal.

wrong.c4: If something happens almost every day, it is the norm, not an anomaly.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the 1980 game?
items.passage: The town's team has lost every championship game in its history, with one exception: a stunning victory in 1980 that fans still talk about.
items.clue: lost every championship game; with one exception
items.hint: How does the 1980 game compare to every other championship?
items.explanation: "With one exception" shows the 1980 win broke a long pattern of losses. That is an anomaly. A tradition or habit would be something that happens regularly.

words.definition: to state something firmly and confidently as true

hero.text: Juniper asserted that the bridge was unsafe and refused to let the parade cross until it was inspected.

words.everyday: In her essay, Keisha asserts that school should start later, then supports her claim with sleep research.

contrast.nonExample: Ben mumbled, "Maybe the answer is twelve? I'm not really sure."
contrast.explanation: Ben is guessing with doubt. To assert something is to state it firmly and confidently.

items.prompt: What does "asserted" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The lawyer asserted that her client had been at home all night.
items.hint: A lawyer in court speaks with confidence about a claim.
items.explanation: The lawyer stated the claim firmly and confidently. That is what assert means.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Galileo ___ that Earth moves around the sun, even though powerful leaders of his time insisted it did not. He did not hedge or apologize; he presented it as fact.
items.clue: did not hedge or apologize; presented it as fact
items.hint: He stated the idea without any doubt.
items.explanation: "Did not hedge" and "presented it as fact" show a firm, confident statement. That is asserting. Whispering suggests caution, and doubting is the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word best shows the speaker's confidence?
items.passage: "This data proves it," the scientist ___, tapping the chart. "Ocean temperatures have risen every decade for fifty years."
items.clue: This data proves it; tapping the chart
items.hint: Suggested and hinted are soft. Which verb is firm?
items.explanation: "Proves" and tapping the chart show strong confidence, so asserted fits. Suggested and hinted are tentative, and wondered shows uncertainty.

wrong.a: Suggested is gentle and tentative, not confident.
wrong.b: Wondered means being unsure.
wrong.d: Hinted means saying something indirectly.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what assert means.

chunks.text: The mayor
asserted with confidence
that the new park would open by June.
asserted, though she had no opinion,

items.hint: Asserting means stating a firm claim.
items.explanation: Stating a claim with confidence is asserting. You can't assert something while having no opinion; asserting requires a firm position.

wrong.c4: Asserting means stating a firm position, so "no opinion" contradicts it.

items.prompt: Is the student asserting a claim?
items.passage: During the debate, Amira said, "I'm not sure, but possibly uniforms might help a little? I could be wrong."
items.hint: Listen for confidence. Does Amira sound firm?
items.explanation: "I'm not sure," "possibly," and "I could be wrong" show doubt. Asserting means stating something firmly as true, so this does not fit.

words.definition: the freedom and ability to make your own decisions and govern yourself

hero.text: After proving she could handle solo patrols, Nova was given autonomy to plan her own routes.

words.everyday: The student council has autonomy over how it spends its budget, as long as it follows school rules.

contrast.nonExample: Every step of the robot's path was programmed by the engineers, and it could not change course.
contrast.explanation: The robot follows instructions with no choice. Autonomy means being free to make your own decisions.

items.prompt: What does "autonomy" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: As a teenager, Lin wanted more autonomy, like choosing her own bedtime and managing her own money.
items.hint: Choosing her own bedtime and managing money are examples. What do they have in common?
items.explanation: Choosing her own bedtime and managing her money are decisions she makes herself. Autonomy is the freedom to decide for yourself.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: For years, the region was ruled by officials sent from the capital. After a peaceful campaign, it won ___ and now elects its own leaders and writes its own laws.
items.clue: elects its own leaders and writes its own laws
items.hint: What does a region have when it governs itself?
items.explanation: Electing its own leaders and writing its own laws means the region governs itself. That is autonomy. Obedience is the opposite: following someone else's rules.

items.prompt: Auto- means "self" (as in autograph), and the Greek root nomos means "law" or "rule." What does autonomy literally mean?
items.hint: Combine self + rule.
items.explanation: Auto- (self) + nomos (rule) = self-rule. A person or group with autonomy makes its own rules and decisions.

wrong.a: Automatic machines share auto-, but the word means self, not machine.
wrong.b: Auto can be short for automobile, but here it means self.
wrong.c: Nomos means law, not name.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what autonomy means.

chunks.text: The art teacher gave students autonomy
over their final projects,
so each chose a subject and medium.
so she chose every color and shape for them.

items.hint: Autonomy means students get to decide.
items.explanation: Letting each student choose a subject and medium gives them autonomy. If the teacher chose everything, students would have no autonomy.

wrong.c4: If the teacher makes every choice, the students have no autonomy.

items.prompt: Which word best completes the passage?
items.passage: The company lets its engineering teams set their own schedules and choose their own projects. Leaders believe this ___ makes employees more creative and committed.
items.clue: set their own schedules and choose their own projects
items.hint: The teams are trusted to make their own choices. That trust is not defiance or neglect.
items.explanation: Setting their own schedules and choosing their own projects is autonomy: freedom given and used responsibly. Rebellion means fighting against authority, but here leaders gave the freedom on purpose.

wrong.a: Working independently doesn't mean being lonely.
wrong.b: Rebellion means resisting authority; here the freedom is granted.
wrong.d: Nothing suggests the teams are careless.

words.definition: hostile and eager to argue or fight

hero.text: Rex stayed calm even when the belligerent villain shouted insults and shoved the barricade.

words.everyday: The belligerent customer pounded the counter and demanded to see the manager over a tiny mistake.

contrast.nonExample: Leah disagreed with her friend's opinion but listened politely and explained her view.
contrast.explanation: Disagreeing calmly is not belligerent. Belligerent means hostile and looking for a fight.

items.prompt: Which person is being belligerent?

options.text: A fan who cheers loudly when his team scores
A player who quietly disagrees with the referee's call
A fan who yells insults and tries to start fights in the stands
A coach who calmly reviews the game film

items.hint: Look for hostility and eagerness to fight.
items.explanation: Yelling insults and trying to start fights is hostile and aggressive, which is belligerent.

wrong.a: Loud cheering is enthusiastic, not hostile.
wrong.b: Disagreeing quietly is not looking for a fight.
wrong.d: Calm reviewing is the opposite of belligerent.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The town meeting was supposed to be a calm discussion, but one ___ resident kept interrupting, jabbing his finger at speakers and daring them to argue.
items.clue: jabbing his finger; daring them to argue
items.hint: How would you describe someone daring others to argue?
items.explanation: Jabbing his finger and daring others to argue show hostility and eagerness to fight. That is belligerent.

items.prompt: Which word best describes Marcus's behavior?
items.passage: When the umpire called him out, Marcus didn't just disagree. He threw his helmet, stormed toward the umpire, and challenged anyone who tried to calm him down.
items.clue: didn't just disagree; challenged anyone
items.hint: Annoyed and disappointed are mild. Which word shows active hostility?
items.explanation: Throwing his helmet and challenging everyone is hostile and combative, so belligerent fits best. Annoyed and disappointed are much milder feelings that don't involve picking fights.

wrong.a: Disappointed describes sadness, not hostility.
wrong.b: Stubborn means refusing to change your mind, not looking for a fight.
wrong.d: Annoyed is too mild for storming and challenging people.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what belligerent means.

chunks.text: The belligerent nation
threatened its neighbors
and massed troops along the border.
and offered them a friendly trade deal.

items.hint: Belligerent means hostile and ready to fight.
items.explanation: Threatening neighbors and massing troops shows a hostile, warlike attitude, which is belligerent. A friendly trade deal is peaceful.

wrong.c4: A friendly trade deal is peaceful, the opposite of belligerent.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly OPPOSITE to "belligerent" in this sentence?
items.passage: The belligerent tone of the letter surprised everyone on the committee.
items.hint: Find the word that means trying to make peace.
items.explanation: Conciliatory means trying to calm things and make peace, the opposite of belligerent. Hostile is a synonym.

wrong.b: Hostile means almost the same as belligerent.
wrong.c: A formal letter could still be belligerent or peaceful.
wrong.d: Length has nothing to do with hostility.

words.definition: to force someone to do something by using threats or pressure

hero.text: The villain tried to coerce Kai into opening the vault by threatening the city's power grid, but Kai refused.

words.everyday: The older students tried to coerce the new kid into giving up his lunch money, so he reported them to a teacher.

contrast.nonExample: Mr. Diaz explained the benefits of joining the band and let each student decide.
contrast.explanation: Persuading with reasons and leaving the choice free is not coercion. Coercing uses threats or pressure to take away real choice.

items.prompt: Is this an example of coercing someone?
items.passage: Tyler told his little sister he would break her toy unless she did his chores.
items.hint: Is Tyler using a threat to make her do something?
items.explanation: Tyler threatens to break the toy to force his sister to do his chores. Using a threat to force someone is coercing.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Historians found that many workers had not signed the contract freely. Factory owners had ___ them by threatening to fire anyone who refused.
items.clue: had not signed freely; threatening to fire anyone who refused
items.hint: The owners used a threat to get signatures.
items.explanation: "Not signed freely" and "threatening to fire" show the workers were forced by threat. That is coerced.

items.prompt: Which word best describes what the club president did?
items.passage: The club president gave a passionate speech, shared survey results, and answered every question. By the end, most members voted for the new plan because they agreed with it.
items.clue: shared survey results; because they agreed with it
items.hint: Did she use threats, or reasons?
items.explanation: She used reasons and evidence, and members genuinely agreed, so she persuaded them. Coerced would mean she used threats or pressure, which the passage does not show.

wrong.a: Coercing involves threats or pressure; the members agreed freely.
wrong.b: Tricking involves deception, and she was open and honest.
wrong.d: Ordering uses authority, but she convinced them with reasons.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what coerce means.

chunks.text: The scammer tried to coerce the man
into paying a fake fine
by threatening to have him arrested.
by politely suggesting it might be nice.

items.hint: Coercion uses threats or pressure.
items.explanation: Threatening arrest to force a payment is coercion. A polite suggestion leaves the choice free, so it isn't coercing.

wrong.c4: A polite suggestion is not a threat or pressure, so it isn't coercion.

items.prompt: Why did the court throw out the confession?
items.passage: The judge ruled that the confession could not be used. Officers had questioned the suspect for twenty hours without food or sleep and warned that his family would suffer if he stayed silent.

options.text: The officers forgot to record it.

items.clue: twenty hours without food or sleep; warned that his family would suffer
items.hint: Look at the pressure and threats the officers used.
items.explanation: Twenty hours without rest and threats about his family are extreme pressure. The confession was coerced, so it was not freely given.

words.definition: too satisfied with yourself or a situation, so you stop trying or ignore possible danger

hero.text: After ten easy wins, Bolt grew complacent and skipped training, so the next challenge caught him off guard.

words.everyday: The team became complacent with a big lead, stopped hustling, and lost in the final minutes.

contrast.nonExample: Even after winning the spelling bee, Aisha kept studying new words every night.
contrast.explanation: Aisha stays hard-working after success. Complacent people stop trying because they feel too comfortable.

items.prompt: What does "complacent" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Because the town hadn't flooded in fifty years, residents grew complacent and stopped clearing the storm drains.
items.hint: Why did they stop clearing the drains?
items.explanation: Feeling safe for so long, residents stopped taking precautions. Complacent means too comfortable or satisfied to stay careful.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The company had dominated the phone market for years. Its leaders became ___, assuming customers would always be loyal, and they ignored a small rival that was quietly building a better product.
items.clue: assuming customers would always be loyal; ignored a small rival
items.hint: Success made the leaders stop paying attention to danger.
items.explanation: Assuming loyalty and ignoring a rival show leaders who were too satisfied to stay alert. That is complacent. Anxious leaders would have watched the rival closely.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the coach's warning?
items.passage: "Being ___ about our skills is good," Coach Lee said, "but being complacent will cost us. Confidence keeps working; complacency stops."
items.clue: Confidence keeps working; complacency stops
items.hint: The coach contrasts a good kind of self-belief with complacency.
items.explanation: The coach says confidence is good, but complacency is not. Both involve feeling sure of yourself, but complacent people stop trying. Lazy and careless are negative, so they don't fit "is good."

wrong.a: The coach says the first word "is good," and lazy is not.
wrong.c: Careless is negative, which clashes with "is good."
wrong.d: Bored doesn't connect to the contrast about skills.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what complacent means.

chunks.text: Having aced the first quiz,
Owen grew complacent
and stopped reviewing his notes.
and studied even harder for the next one.

items.hint: Complacent people stop putting in effort after success.
items.explanation: Stopping review after a good grade shows Owen got too comfortable. Studying harder would show the opposite of complacency.

wrong.c4: Studying even harder shows drive, the opposite of complacent.

items.prompt: Is this an example of being complacent?
items.passage: Although the hospital had passed every safety inspection for a decade, its staff still practiced emergency drills every month and updated their plans each year.
items.hint: Did their success make them stop being careful?
items.explanation: Despite a long record of success, the staff keeps practicing and updating plans. They stay alert, which is the opposite of complacent.

words.definition: an opinion or guess formed without complete evidence

hero.text: Juniper's idea that the thief used the rooftops was only conjecture until Pixel found footprints on the roof.

words.everyday: Scientists once believed Mars had canals, but that was conjecture based on blurry telescope images.

contrast.nonExample: The thermometer read exactly 22 degrees Celsius.
contrast.explanation: A direct measurement is a confirmed fact. A conjecture is a guess made without complete proof.

items.prompt: What does "conjecture" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: No one knows why the ancient city was abandoned; every explanation so far is conjecture.
items.hint: "No one knows" tells you something about the explanations.
items.explanation: Since no one knows, each explanation is a guess without complete evidence. That is conjecture.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The reporter's claim that the mayor would resign was pure ___. She had no sources, no documents, and no statement from the mayor's office.
items.clue: no sources, no documents, and no statement
items.hint: A claim with no support at all is what kind of thing?
items.explanation: With no sources, documents, or statements, the claim was a guess. That is conjecture. Evidence, testimony, and data are all forms of support she lacked.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the scientist's careful wording?
items.passage: "We haven't tested this yet," Dr. Reyes said, "so for now, the idea that the bees navigate using sunlight is only a ___."
items.clue: We haven't tested this yet; only
items.hint: Rumor and conjecture are both unproven. Which suggests reasoned thinking rather than gossip?
items.explanation: Conjecture is a reasoned guess without full proof, which fits an untested scientific idea. A rumor is gossip passed from person to person. Law and conclusion suggest the idea is already proven.

wrong.a: A scientific law is well established, not untested.
wrong.b: A conclusion comes after testing, not before.
wrong.c: A rumor is unverified gossip, not a scientist's reasoned idea.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what conjecture means.

chunks.text: The idea that the painting was by Rembrandt
remained conjecture
until experts tested the paint and canvas.
because experts had already proven it beyond doubt.

items.hint: Conjecture lasts until proof arrives.
items.explanation: The idea was a guess until testing gave evidence, so it remained conjecture until then. Something proven beyond doubt is no longer conjecture.

wrong.c4: If it was proven beyond doubt, it was a fact, not conjecture.

items.prompt: Is the student's statement a conjecture?
items.passage: After noticing that 1+3=4, 1+3+5=9, and 1+3+5+7=16, Talia said, "I think adding odd numbers in order always gives a perfect square, but I haven't proven it."
items.hint: Does Talia have complete proof, or a reasoned guess?
items.explanation: Talia sees a pattern and makes a guess, but says she hasn't proven it. In math, an unproven statement based on a pattern is called a conjecture.

words.definition: the feeling or idea a word suggests beyond its basic dictionary meaning

hero.text: Nova told reporters the team was "determined," not "stubborn," because she liked the positive connotation.

words.everyday: "Thrifty" and "cheap" both mean careful with money, but "cheap" has a negative connotation.

contrast.nonExample: The dictionary defines "house" as a building where people live.
contrast.explanation: That is the denotation, the literal meaning. A connotation is the extra feeling a word carries, like "home" suggesting warmth.

items.prompt: What does "connotation" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: "Slender" and "skinny" both mean thin, but "slender" has a more flattering connotation.
items.hint: Both words mean thin. What is different about them?
items.explanation: The words share a dictionary meaning, but "slender" feels more positive. That extra feeling is its connotation. The dictionary definition is the denotation.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The ad called the apartment "cozy" instead of "cramped." Both words describe a small space, but the advertiser chose the one with the warmer ___.
items.clue: Both words describe a small space; warmer
items.hint: Same meaning, different feeling. What is the feeling called?
items.explanation: Cozy and cramped describe the same size, but cozy feels warmer. That feeling is the word's connotation.

items.prompt: A biographer admires her subject. Which word has the most positive connotation?
items.passage: As a young inventor, Hedy Lamarr was ___; she refused to give up on her ideas even when experts dismissed them.
items.clue: admires her subject
items.hint: All four mean not giving up. Which one sounds like praise?
items.explanation: All four words share a basic meaning, but persistent has a positive connotation of admirable effort. Stubborn, pig-headed, and obstinate suggest someone unreasonable.

wrong.a: Stubborn often suggests being unreasonable.
wrong.b: Pig-headed is clearly insulting.
wrong.d: Obstinate suggests refusing to listen, a negative connotation.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what connotation means.

chunks.text: The word "childlike"
has a positive connotation of innocence,
while "childish" suggests immaturity.
because it has exactly nine letters.

items.hint: Connotation is about feeling, not letters.
items.explanation: Childlike and childish share a root, but one suggests innocence and the other immaturity. Those feelings are connotations. Letter count has nothing to do with connotation.

wrong.c4: A word's length is not its connotation; connotation is the feeling it carries.

items.prompt: Why did the editor change the word?
items.passage: In a news story about a protest, a reporter wrote that the crowd "swarmed" the square. The editor changed it to "gathered in," explaining that "swarmed" made people sound like insects attacking.
items.clue: made people sound like insects attacking
items.hint: What feeling did "swarmed" add?
items.explanation: "Swarmed" suggests insects attacking, a negative feeling beyond its literal meaning. The editor removed it because of that connotation, choosing neutral language for a news story.

words.definition: very easy to notice; standing out clearly

hero.text: Rex's bright orange cape made him conspicuous on the stealth mission, so he swapped it for a dark one.

words.everyday: The one red tulip was conspicuous in a field of white ones.

contrast.nonExample: The moth's gray wings blended perfectly into the tree bark.
contrast.explanation: The moth is camouflaged and hard to see. Conspicuous means easy to notice.

items.prompt: Is the student conspicuous?
items.passage: At a school where everyone wears navy uniforms, Felix shows up in a bright yellow suit.
items.hint: Would Felix be easy to spot?
items.explanation: A bright yellow suit among navy uniforms stands out immediately. That is conspicuous.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The spy tried to look ordinary, but his ___ behavior gave him away. He checked over his shoulder every few seconds and wore sunglasses indoors.
items.clue: gave him away; sunglasses indoors
items.hint: His behavior made him easy to notice.
items.explanation: Checking over his shoulder and wearing sunglasses indoors made him stand out. That is conspicuous. Ordinary is what he wanted to be.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly OPPOSITE to "conspicuous" in this sentence?
items.passage: The new skyscraper is the most conspicuous building in the city skyline.
items.hint: The prefix in- often means not.
items.explanation: Inconspicuous means not easy to notice, the opposite of conspicuous. Prominent is a synonym.

wrong.b: Prominent means standing out, almost the same as conspicuous.
wrong.c: Cost has nothing to do with being noticeable.
wrong.d: A modern building could be conspicuous or not.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what conspicuous means.

chunks.text: The coffee stain on his white shirt
was so conspicuous
that everyone noticed it right away.
that no one could find it.

items.hint: Conspicuous things get noticed.
items.explanation: A conspicuous stain is easy to see, so everyone noticed it. If no one could find it, it would be inconspicuous.

wrong.c4: If no one could find it, the stain was hidden, not conspicuous.

items.prompt: Which word best completes the passage?
items.passage: In the class photo, everyone is smiling except Marco, whose frown is ___. It is the first thing viewers notice.
items.clue: everyone is smiling except Marco; the first thing viewers notice
items.hint: Flashy and conspicuous both relate to standing out. Which fits a frown?
items.explanation: Marco's frown stands out because it differs from everyone else's smile, so it is conspicuous. Flashy suggests bright, showy display meant to impress, which doesn't fit a frown.

wrong.a: Flashy means showy and attention-seeking, not just noticeable.
wrong.c: Faint means hard to notice, the opposite.
wrong.d: Secretive means hiding things.

words.definition: to reach a final high point or end result after building up over time

hero.text: Months of training culminated in Pixel's first solo rescue.

words.everyday: The science unit culminated in a fair where students presented their experiments to parents.

contrast.nonExample: On the first day of the course, students received their textbooks.
contrast.explanation: That is a beginning, not a peak. Culminate describes the final high point of a long process.

items.prompt: What does "culminated" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Years of protests culminated in a new law protecting voting rights.
items.hint: What happened at the end of years of protests?
items.explanation: After years of building effort, the protests led to a final outcome: a new law. Culminated means reached a final high point or result.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The symphony builds slowly, adding instruments one by one. It finally ___ in a thunderous finale with the full orchestra and a choir.
items.clue: builds slowly; finally; thunderous finale
items.hint: The music builds and ends at a peak.
items.explanation: "Builds slowly" and "finally" lead to a "thunderous finale," the high point. That is culminates. Begins describes the start, not the peak.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the passage?
items.passage: The town's year-long celebration of its 200th birthday ___ in a grand parade and fireworks over the river.
items.clue: year-long; grand parade and fireworks
items.hint: Ended is close but plain. Which word shows the ending was a peak?
items.explanation: Culminated means ended at a high point after building up, which fits a grand parade with fireworks. Ended and stopped just mean finished, without the sense of a climax. Quit suggests giving up.

wrong.a: Stopped is neutral and doesn't show a peak.
wrong.b: Ended is close, but it misses the sense of reaching a high point.
wrong.d: Quit suggests giving up partway.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what culminate means.

chunks.text: Her four years of practice
culminated in
a solo performance at the state finals.
her very first piano lesson.

items.hint: Culminate points to a final high point, not a beginning.
items.explanation: After four years, a solo at state finals is the peak of her work. Her first lesson came at the start, so practice couldn't culminate in it.

wrong.c4: A first lesson is a beginning; years of practice can't culminate in a starting point.

items.prompt: Which word best describes how the plot of the novel works?
items.passage: Tension in the novel rises chapter by chapter as secrets pile up. Everything comes to a head in the final scene, when the whole family confronts the truth at last.
items.clue: rises chapter by chapter; comes to a head in the final scene
items.hint: Where does the rising tension end up?
items.explanation: The tension builds and "comes to a head" at the end, which means the plot culminates in a final confrontation. It doesn't begin there or fade away.

words.definition: believing that people are mostly selfish and that their good actions hide bad motives

hero.text: The cynical reporter assumed Juniper only saved the train for the publicity, until he learned she'd asked to stay anonymous.

words.everyday: When the company donated to the hospital, cynical neighbors said it was only trying to look good after a scandal.

contrast.nonExample: Tara assumed her new classmates would be kind and offered to help them.
contrast.explanation: Tara trusts others' good intentions. A cynical person suspects selfish motives behind kindness.

items.prompt: Which comment is cynical?

options.text: "The volunteers cleaned the park because they care about our town."
"I wonder how long the cleanup took."
"Those volunteers only showed up so they could post photos online."

items.hint: Look for the comment that assumes a selfish motive behind a good deed.
items.explanation: Assuming volunteers helped only to show off online is cynical: it treats a good deed as hiding a selfish motive.

wrong.a: This trusts the volunteers' good intentions.
wrong.b: This is a neutral question, not a judgment of motives.
wrong.d: This shows enthusiasm, not distrust.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: After years of broken campaign promises, many voters became ___. They assumed every politician was lying, even ones with honest records.
items.clue: assumed every politician was lying, even ones with honest records
items.hint: The voters now distrust everyone, even honest people.
items.explanation: Assuming everyone is lying, even people with honest records, is cynical. Hopeful and grateful show the opposite attitude.

items.prompt: Which word best describes Noor's reaction?
items.passage: When the ad claimed the cereal "cures tiredness," Noor asked to see the scientific studies before believing it. She didn't assume the company was lying; she just wanted evidence.
items.clue: didn't assume the company was lying; just wanted evidence
items.hint: Cynical people assume the worst. Did Noor?
items.explanation: Noor questions the claim and wants evidence but doesn't assume bad motives, which is skeptical. Cynical would mean she assumed the company was dishonest. Skeptics doubt; cynics distrust.

wrong.b: A cynical person would assume the company was lying, which Noor did not.
wrong.c: Gullible means believing too easily; Noor asked for proof.
wrong.d: Nothing shows Noor was angry or aggressive.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what cynical means.

chunks.text: When the star athlete visited the hospital,
a cynical fan claimed
it was just a stunt to improve his image.
it showed what a generous person he was.

items.hint: A cynic suspects a selfish reason behind kindness.
items.explanation: Calling the visit a stunt for his image assumes a selfish motive, which is cynical. Praising his generosity is trusting, not cynical.

wrong.c4: Praising his generosity trusts his motives, the opposite of cynical.

items.prompt: Which line uses "cynical" naturally?

options.text: "I know it sounds cynical, but I think the contest is just a way to collect our email addresses."
"She's so cynical; she believes everything people tell her."
"The weather was cynical today, with lots of sunshine."
"He felt cynical about winning, so he trained extra hard."

items.hint: Cynical means suspecting a hidden, selfish motive.
items.explanation: Suspecting the contest secretly exists to collect emails assumes a selfish hidden motive, which is cynical. Believing everything is trusting, and weather can't have motives.

wrong.b: Believing everything is the opposite of cynical.
wrong.c: Weather can't be cynical; the word describes attitudes about people's motives.
wrong.d: Cynical isn't a word for feeling eager or determined.

words.definition: working hard with steady, careful effort over time

hero.text: Kai was diligent about practicing his flying drills every morning, even on weekends.

words.everyday: The diligent volunteer showed up every Saturday for two years to restore the old trail.

contrast.nonExample: Sophie crammed for one night before the test and forgot everything a week later.
contrast.explanation: One night of cramming is a burst, not steady effort. Diligent means working consistently and carefully over time.

items.prompt: What does "diligent" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Because she was diligent, Marisol checked her rain gauge at the same time every day for the entire year.
items.hint: She did the same task every day for a whole year.
items.explanation: Checking the gauge every day for a year shows steady, careful effort. That is diligent.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Marie Curie was famously ___. She spent four years stirring huge pots of ore by hand, processing tons of material to isolate a tiny amount of radium.
items.clue: four years stirring huge pots; processing tons of material
items.hint: Years of hard, repetitive work describes what kind of person?
items.explanation: Four years of hard, steady work to get a tiny result shows diligence. Impatient people would have quit long before.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the teacher's praise?
items.passage: "Jun isn't the fastest learner," the teacher wrote, "but he is the most ___ student I've had. He completes every assignment carefully and asks for feedback each week."
items.clue: isn't the fastest learner, but; completes every assignment carefully
items.hint: The teacher praises effort, not talent or simply following orders.
items.explanation: Diligent describes steady, careful effort, which matches completing every assignment carefully. Gifted is about natural talent, which the teacher says Jun lacks. Busy just means having lots to do; obedient means following orders.

wrong.a: Gifted means naturally talented, but the teacher praises effort instead.
wrong.b: Busy doesn't mean careful or hardworking.
wrong.d: Obedient means following orders, not taking initiative to ask for feedback.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what diligent means.

chunks.text: The diligent apprentice
practiced carving every evening for months
until her bowls were smooth and even.
until she got bored after a day and quit.

items.hint: Diligent means steady effort over time.
items.explanation: Practicing every evening for months until the work improved shows diligence. Quitting after a day shows the opposite.

wrong.c4: Quitting after one day is not steady effort, so it contradicts diligent.

items.prompt: Is this an example of being diligent?
items.passage: Andre was supposed to water the school garden daily, but he only remembered when the plants began to wilt.
items.hint: Is Andre's effort steady and careful?
items.explanation: Andre only waters when there is a problem, so his effort is not steady. Diligent means consistent, careful work, so this does not fit.

words.definition: to notice, recognize, or tell apart something that is hard to see or understand

hero.text: Through the thick fog, Nova could just discern the outline of a boat drifting toward the rocks.

words.everyday: A trained musician can discern the difference between two notes that sound identical to most people.

contrast.nonExample: Everyone could see the giant billboard from a mile away.
contrast.explanation: Seeing something obvious takes no special effort. Discern means picking out something subtle or hard to detect.

items.prompt: What does "discern" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: In the dim cave, the scientists could barely discern the shapes painted on the wall.
items.hint: In dim light, what is hard to do with the shapes?
items.explanation: In dim light, the scientists could barely make out the shapes. Discern means to notice or recognize something hard to see.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The two paintings look nearly identical, but an expert can ___ the forgery by examining tiny differences in the brushwork.
items.clue: nearly identical; tiny differences
items.hint: The expert has to tell apart two things that look the same.
items.explanation: "Nearly identical" and "tiny differences" show that telling the paintings apart takes skill. Discern means to recognize or tell apart something subtle.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the passage?
items.passage: Reading the letter several times, Ms. Kim began to ___ a note of sadness beneath its cheerful words.
items.clue: Reading the letter several times; beneath its cheerful words
items.hint: The sadness is hidden. Which word suggests careful, perceptive noticing?
items.explanation: Discern means perceiving something subtle, like a hidden feeling, through careful attention. See is too general, and glance at is too quick. Invent would mean the sadness isn't really there.

wrong.a: See is too plain; it doesn't capture noticing something hidden.
wrong.c: A glance is too quick to catch a hidden tone.
wrong.d: Invent means making it up, but the sadness is really in the letter.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what discern means.

chunks.text: Using a powerful telescope,
the astronomer could discern
a faint moon circling the distant planet.
the huge, bright sun at noon without trying.

items.hint: Discern is used for things that are hard to detect.
items.explanation: A faint, distant moon is hard to detect, so discern fits. The noon sun is obvious, so discerning it makes no sense.

wrong.c4: The sun at noon is obvious; discern is for something subtle or hard to detect.

items.prompt: What skill does the passage describe?
items.passage: Good readers of the news learn to discern fact from opinion. They notice when a writer slips a personal judgment into what looks like neutral reporting.

options.text: telling apart things that are easily confused

items.clue: notice when a writer slips a personal judgment into what looks like neutral reporting
items.hint: What do good readers notice that others might miss?
items.explanation: Spotting a hidden judgment in what looks neutral means telling apart fact and opinion, two things easily confused. That is discerning.

words.definition: a large and often unfair difference between two or more things

hero.text: Bolt noticed a disparity in the academy's budget: the flight team got new gear every year, while the medical team still used old equipment.

words.everyday: The report revealed a disparity in test scores between schools with libraries and schools without them.

contrast.nonExample: The twins scored 88 and 89 on the same test.
contrast.explanation: A one-point gap is small. A disparity is a large, noticeable difference, often one that seems unfair.

items.prompt: Does this situation show a disparity?
items.passage: In one town, the wealthy neighborhood has three parks and a pool, while the neighborhood across the river has no parks at all.
items.hint: Is there a large, unequal difference?
items.explanation: Three parks and a pool versus none is a big, unfair difference. That is a disparity.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: In 1900, factory owners earned thousands of dollars a year while many child workers earned only pennies a day. Reformers pointed to this ___ as proof that new labor laws were needed.
items.clue: thousands of dollars a year; only pennies a day
items.hint: Compare the owners' pay to the children's pay.
items.explanation: Thousands of dollars versus pennies is a huge, unfair gap. That is a disparity. Similarity is the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the reporter's concerned tone?
items.passage: The study found a troubling ___ in health care: rural patients waited three times longer for treatment than city patients.
items.clue: troubling; three times longer
items.hint: Variation and contrast are neutral. Which word suggests the difference is unfair?
items.explanation: Disparity names a large difference that is often unfair, which matches "troubling." Variation and contrast describe differences neutrally, without suggesting a problem.

wrong.a: Variation is neutral; it doesn't suggest unfairness.
wrong.c: Contrast is neutral and often used for comparisons in art or writing.
wrong.d: A detail is a small fact, not a gap between groups.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what disparity means.

chunks.text: There is a wide disparity
between the two teams' budgets:
one spends ten times more than the other.
both spend almost exactly the same amount.

items.hint: A disparity is a big difference.
items.explanation: Spending ten times more shows a large gap, which is a disparity. Spending the same amount is equality, not disparity.

wrong.c4: Spending the same amount shows equality, the opposite of a disparity.

items.prompt: In disparity, dis- means "not," and the root par means "equal" (as in on par). What does disparity mean?

options.text: a state of being not equal

items.hint: Put the parts together: not + equal.
items.explanation: Dis- (not) + par (equal) = not equal. A disparity is an inequality or large gap between things.

wrong.a: Disparity has nothing to do with a party, even though it contains those letters.
wrong.c: Sharing would reduce a disparity, not define it.
wrong.d: Disparity is unrelated to disappear.

words.definition: able to speak or write in a clear, powerful, and moving way

hero.text: Juniper gave an eloquent speech at the memorial, and even the toughest heroes wiped away tears.

words.everyday: Frederick Douglass's eloquent writing persuaded many readers to join the fight against slavery.

contrast.nonExample: Max mumbled through his book report, saying "um" after every few words and losing his place.
contrast.explanation: Mumbling and losing your place is unclear speech. Eloquent speech is clear, graceful, and persuasive.

items.prompt: What does "eloquent" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The eloquent student convinced the school board to keep the music program with a short, moving speech.
items.hint: Her short speech was moving and convincing.
items.explanation: She convinced the board with a moving speech, so she spoke clearly and powerfully. That is eloquent. Being loud is not the same as being eloquent.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address is only about 270 words long, yet it is considered one of the most ___ speeches in American history; its simple, powerful phrases are still quoted today.
items.clue: simple, powerful phrases are still quoted today
items.hint: A short speech that people still quote must be powerful.
items.explanation: "Simple, powerful phrases" still quoted today show the speech is clear and moving. That is eloquent. Lengthy contradicts "only about 270 words."

items.prompt: Which word best fits the passage?
items.passage: The salesman talked fast and smoothly, but his pitch felt slippery and insincere. He was ___, not truly eloquent.
items.clue: fast and smoothly; slippery and insincere; not truly eloquent
items.hint: You need a word for smooth talk that lacks sincerity.
items.explanation: Glib means smooth and easy-talking but shallow or insincere. The passage contrasts that with eloquent, which is powerful and genuine. Moving would actually describe eloquent speech.

wrong.b: The passage calls his pitch insincere, so honest doesn't fit.
wrong.c: He talked fast, so he wasn't silent.
wrong.d: Moving describes eloquent speech, which the passage says he lacked.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what eloquent means.

chunks.text: The poet's eloquent words
captured the grief of the whole town
so perfectly that listeners wept.
so poorly that no one understood them.

items.hint: Eloquent words are clear and moving.
items.explanation: Words that capture grief so well that people weep are powerful and moving, which is eloquent. Words no one understood would not be eloquent.

wrong.c4: If no one understood the words, they were unclear, not eloquent.

items.prompt: The Latin root loqu means "speak," as in loquacious (very talkative). Which word shares the root in eloquent?
items.hint: Look for loqu in the word, and a meaning connected to speaking.
items.explanation: Soliloquy (a speech a character gives alone) contains loqu, meaning speak, just like eloquent. Elegant and elevator start the same way but have no connection to speaking.

wrong.a: Elevator comes from a root meaning lift.
wrong.b: Local comes from a root meaning place.
wrong.c: Elegant sounds similar but doesn't contain loqu or relate to speech.

words.definition: based on observation, experiment, or experience rather than theory or opinion alone

hero.text: Pixel wanted empirical proof that the new shield worked, so she tested it fifty times in the lab.

words.everyday: The class gathered empirical evidence about plant growth by measuring their seedlings every day.

contrast.nonExample: Marcus believes cats are smarter than dogs because it just feels true to him.
contrast.explanation: A feeling or belief isn't based on observation. Empirical evidence comes from measuring, testing, or observing.

items.prompt: Is this empirical evidence?
items.passage: To find out which paper towel is most absorbent, Grace soaks five brands in water and measures how much each one holds.
items.hint: Is Grace testing and measuring, or just guessing?
items.explanation: Grace runs a test and measures the results. Evidence from observation and experiment is empirical.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Ancient thinkers argued that heavy objects fall faster than light ones, but few tested the idea. Later scientists insisted on ___ evidence, so they dropped objects and timed their falls.
items.clue: few tested the idea; dropped objects and timed their falls
items.hint: The later scientists wanted evidence from actual experiments.
items.explanation: Dropping objects and timing them produces evidence from observation and experiment. That is empirical evidence, unlike the untested arguments of ancient thinkers.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly OPPOSITE to "empirical" in this sentence?
items.passage: The researcher's conclusions were empirical, drawn from years of field observations.
items.hint: Empirical is based on observation. What is based on ideas alone?
items.explanation: Theoretical means based on ideas or reasoning without direct observation, the opposite of empirical. Measured is a near-synonym.

wrong.a: Measured is close in meaning to empirical.
wrong.c: Empirical conclusions can be accurate; this is not an opposite.
wrong.d: Scientific work is often empirical, so this is not an opposite.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what empirical means.

chunks.text: The doctors relied on empirical data
collected from thousands of patients
during a three-year clinical trial.
imagined by one doctor during a daydream.

items.hint: Empirical data comes from real observation.
items.explanation: Data collected from thousands of patients in a trial comes from observation and experiment, so it is empirical. Imagined data is not.

wrong.c4: Something imagined in a daydream is not based on observation, so it isn't empirical.

items.prompt: Which word best completes the passage?
items.passage: Before planting, the farmer didn't rely on old sayings about the moon. She kept records of rainfall, temperature, and harvests for ten years, and made decisions based on that ___ knowledge.
items.clue: didn't rely on old sayings; kept records for ten years
items.hint: Her knowledge comes from careful records, not sayings.
items.explanation: Ten years of records on rainfall and harvests is knowledge based on observation, which is empirical. Traditional knowledge, like old sayings, is what she chose not to rely on.

wrong.a: Traditional knowledge is what she rejected (the old sayings).
wrong.c: Nothing about her records is magical.
wrong.d: Her records aren't described as hidden.

words.definition: a mistaken belief, or an error in reasoning that makes an argument unsound

hero.text: Kai spotted the fallacy in the villain's argument: just because the city was calm yesterday didn't mean it was safe today.

words.everyday: It's a common fallacy that we only use ten percent of our brains; scans show activity throughout the brain.

contrast.nonExample: All mammals breathe air. Whales are mammals. So whales breathe air.
contrast.explanation: That reasoning is sound: the conclusion follows from true facts. A fallacy is a flaw in reasoning or a false belief.

items.prompt: What does "fallacy" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: It is a fallacy that lightning never strikes the same place twice; tall buildings are hit many times a year.
items.hint: The second part of the sentence proves the belief wrong.
items.explanation: The belief is proven false by buildings being hit many times. A fallacy is a mistaken belief.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: "Everyone at school has a phone, so phones must be good for kids," Jordan argued. His teacher pointed out the ___: something being popular doesn't prove it is good.
items.clue: something being popular doesn't prove it is good
items.hint: The teacher found a flaw in Jordan's reasoning.
items.explanation: The teacher explains that popularity doesn't prove goodness, so Jordan's argument has a reasoning error. That is a fallacy.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the passage?
items.passage: Leila typed 4,500 instead of 45,000 in her spreadsheet. Her calculation was wrong, but her reasoning was fine. It was a simple ___, not a fallacy.
items.clue: her reasoning was fine; not a fallacy
items.hint: A fallacy is an error in reasoning. What kind of mistake is a mistyped number?
items.explanation: Mistyping a number is a typo, an accident of entry. A fallacy is a flaw in reasoning or a false belief, which the passage says Leila didn't have.

wrong.a: She didn't propose a theory.
wrong.b: Her argument was fine; the mistake was a typing error.
wrong.d: Her mistake wasn't a belief; she just pressed the wrong keys.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what fallacy means.

chunks.text: It is a fallacy
that cold weather alone causes colds;
colds are actually caused by viruses.
and scientists have proven this belief completely true.

items.hint: A fallacy is a belief that turns out to be wrong.
items.explanation: The belief that cold weather alone causes colds is mistaken, because viruses cause them. That makes it a fallacy. A belief proven true can't be a fallacy.

wrong.c4: If a belief is proven true, it isn't a fallacy.

items.prompt: Does this argument contain a fallacy?
items.passage: "I wore my lucky socks and we won the game. So my socks made us win, and I should wear them every game."
items.hint: Does wearing socks before a win prove the socks caused the win?
items.explanation: Two things happening together doesn't prove one caused the other. Assuming the socks caused the win is a reasoning error, so the argument contains a fallacy.

words.definition: not serious or important; silly or wasteful when something more serious is needed

hero.text: During the emergency briefing, Bolt's frivolous jokes annoyed the team, who needed to focus.

words.everyday: The judge dismissed the frivolous lawsuit, which demanded a million dollars because a pizza arrived five minutes late.

contrast.nonExample: The town council spent the money on repairing the leaking school roof.
contrast.explanation: Fixing a leaking roof is serious and necessary. Frivolous describes things that are silly or unimportant when seriousness is needed.

items.prompt: Which purchase is frivolous?

options.text: Buying a winter coat when your old one is too small
Buying medicine for a sick pet
Buying a gold-plated phone case with savings meant for rent

items.hint: Look for the silly, unnecessary choice when money is needed for something serious.
items.explanation: A gold-plated phone case is unnecessary, and using rent money makes it wasteful. That is frivolous. The other purchases meet real needs.

wrong.a: A coat that fits is a real need.
wrong.b: Medicine for a sick pet is important.
wrong.d: Groceries are a basic need.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: With the city facing a water shortage, residents were angry that officials spent the meeting debating the color of new parking signs. To them, it seemed ___.
items.clue: facing a water shortage; debating the color of parking signs
items.hint: Compare the serious problem to what officials discussed.
items.explanation: Debating sign colors during a water shortage seems silly and unimportant compared to the real crisis. That is frivolous. Urgent and essential describe the water shortage, not the sign debate.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the passage's positive tone?
items.passage: After months of exams, the class spent a ___ afternoon at the beach, building sandcastles and laughing. Everyone agreed they had earned it.
items.clue: Everyone agreed they had earned it
items.hint: Frivolous suggests the fun was a waste. Which word sounds approving?
items.explanation: Carefree describes lighthearted fun in a positive way. Frivolous, wasteful, and pointless all suggest the afternoon was silly or wrong, but the passage says they earned it.

wrong.a: Frivolous carries criticism, suggesting the fun wasn't deserved.
wrong.b: Wasteful is negative, but the passage approves.
wrong.d: Pointless is negative and clashes with "earned it."

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what frivolous means.

chunks.text: The principal rejected the frivolous request
to cancel classes
so students could watch a cartoon marathon.
because a dangerous blizzard was approaching.

items.hint: A frivolous request is silly, not serious.
items.explanation: Canceling school for a cartoon marathon is silly and unimportant, so the request was frivolous. Canceling for a dangerous blizzard is serious and reasonable.

wrong.c4: A dangerous blizzard is a serious reason, so the request wouldn't be frivolous.

items.prompt: How does the reviewer feel about the musical?
items.passage: The musical tackles a serious subject, the Great Depression, but treats it with frivolous song-and-dance numbers about fancy hats. The reviewer felt it made light of real suffering.

options.text: It was too serious and sad.
It was too silly for its subject.

items.clue: serious subject; songs about fancy hats; made light of real suffering
items.hint: What is the mismatch between the topic and the songs?
items.explanation: Silly songs about fancy hats for a story about the Great Depression "made light of real suffering." The reviewer finds the musical frivolous, too silly for a serious subject.

words.definition: a system in which people or things are ranked one above another by importance or power

hero.text: In the academy's hierarchy, cadets report to team leaders, and team leaders report to Commander Rex.

words.everyday: In medieval Europe, the social hierarchy placed kings at the top, then nobles, then knights, with peasants at the bottom.

contrast.nonExample: In the study group, everyone shares ideas equally and no one is in charge.
contrast.explanation: A group where everyone is equal has no ranks. A hierarchy ranks members from higher to lower.

items.prompt: Is this an example of a hierarchy?
items.passage: In a wolf pack, the lead pair eats first, then the older wolves, and the youngest eat last.
items.hint: Are the wolves ranked from top to bottom?
items.explanation: The wolves follow a clear order from the lead pair down to the youngest. A ranking system like this is a hierarchy.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: In the restaurant kitchen, the head chef gives orders to the sous-chef, who directs the line cooks, who supervise the dishwashers. Everyone knows their place in the ___.
items.clue: gives orders to; directs; supervise
items.hint: Each person is above or below someone else.
items.explanation: Each worker gives orders to the one below, forming ranked levels. That is a hierarchy. In a democracy, people would share power more equally.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the science passage?
items.passage: Biologists classify living things in a ___ of groups: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, and species, from broadest to most specific.
