items.clue: from broadest to most specific
items.hint: Collection and pile are groups without order. Which word shows ranked levels?
items.explanation: The groups are arranged in levels from broadest to most specific, so they form a hierarchy. A collection or pile has no ranked levels.

wrong.a: A collection is a group with no built-in ranking.
wrong.b: A pile is disorganized.
wrong.d: A mixture has no ordered levels.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what hierarchy means.

chunks.text: In the army's strict hierarchy,
privates follow orders from sergeants,
who answer to officers above them.
and every soldier has exactly the same rank.

items.hint: A hierarchy has levels, one above another.
items.explanation: Privates, sergeants, and officers form ranked levels, which is a hierarchy. If everyone had the same rank, there would be no hierarchy.

wrong.c4: If everyone has the same rank, there are no levels, so there is no hierarchy.

items.prompt: What does the passage suggest about the startup company?
items.passage: At the small startup, there are no managers or job titles. Interns and founders sit at the same table, and anyone can propose or reject an idea.

options.text: It has a very strict hierarchy.

items.clue: no managers or job titles; anyone can propose or reject an idea
items.hint: Is anyone ranked above anyone else?
items.explanation: No managers, no titles, and equal say for everyone mean there are no ranked levels. The company has almost no hierarchy.

words.definition: about to happen very soon, often in a threatening way

hero.text: When the volcano began to rumble and smoke, Nova knew an eruption was imminent and evacuated the village.

words.everyday: Dark clouds rolled in and thunder boomed; rain was clearly imminent, so the umpire stopped the game.

contrast.nonExample: Scientists predict the sun will run out of fuel in about five billion years.
contrast.explanation: Five billion years away is not soon. Imminent means about to happen any moment.

items.prompt: What does "imminent" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The weather service warned that a tornado was imminent and told everyone to take shelter immediately.
items.hint: Why would people need to take shelter immediately?
items.explanation: People must take shelter immediately because the tornado is about to arrive. Imminent means about to happen very soon.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The old dam groaned, and water sprayed through widening cracks. Engineers said its failure was ___ and ordered the town below evacuated within the hour.
items.clue: widening cracks; evacuated within the hour
items.hint: How soon do engineers expect the dam to fail?
items.explanation: Widening cracks and an evacuation "within the hour" show failure was about to happen. That is imminent. Distant means far in the future.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the passage?
items.passage: The school board will vote on the new calendar sometime next spring. A decision is ___, but not imminent.
items.clue: sometime next spring; but not imminent
items.hint: The decision will come, but not right away.
items.explanation: Expected means it will happen but doesn't say how soon, which matches "next spring." Imminent means any moment now, and urgent, sudden, and immediate all suggest something happening right away.

wrong.a: Urgent suggests it must happen right now.
wrong.c: Sudden means happening quickly and without warning.
wrong.d: Immediate means right now, which contradicts "next spring."

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what imminent means.

chunks.text: With the timer showing ten seconds left,
the rocket launch
was imminent.
was still several years away.

items.hint: Imminent means it will happen very soon.
items.explanation: Ten seconds left means the launch is about to happen, so it is imminent. Several years away is the opposite.

wrong.c4: Several years away is distant, not imminent, and it clashes with ten seconds left.

items.prompt: Which line uses "imminent" naturally?

options.text: "The dinosaurs' extinction was imminent 66 million years ago, and it's imminent still."
"My birthday is imminent; it's in eleven months."
"The bus is pulling up now, so our departure is imminent. Grab your bags!"
"She wore an imminent jacket to the party."

items.hint: Find the event that is about to happen right now.
items.explanation: A bus pulling up means departure will happen any moment, so imminent fits. Eleven months is far away, and a jacket can't be about to happen.

wrong.a: An event 66 million years ago is in the past, not about to happen.
wrong.b: Eleven months away is too far off to be imminent.
wrong.d: Imminent describes events, not clothing.

words.definition: continuing without stopping, often in an annoying way

hero.text: The incessant beeping of the broken alarm made it impossible for Pixel to concentrate.

words.everyday: The incessant rain lasted eleven days and flooded the farmers' fields.

contrast.nonExample: The church bell rings once every hour.
contrast.explanation: A bell that rings once an hour stops in between. Incessant means it never lets up.

items.prompt: Is this noise incessant?
items.passage: A neighbor's dog barks a few times when the mail carrier arrives each afternoon, then goes quiet.
items.hint: Does the barking keep going without stopping?
items.explanation: The dog barks a few times and then stops. Incessant means continuing without a break, so this does not fit.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Living next to the construction site was exhausting. The ___ pounding of jackhammers began at dawn and didn't pause until long after dark.
items.clue: began at dawn and didn't pause until long after dark
items.hint: The noise never takes a break all day.
items.explanation: "Didn't pause" from dawn until after dark shows the noise never stopped. That is incessant. Occasional and brief describe the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word best captures the annoyed tone?
items.passage: On the long car ride, her little brother's ___ questions ("Are we there yet? Why? How much longer?") drove everyone crazy.
items.clue: drove everyone crazy
items.hint: Frequent and regular are neutral. Which word suggests the questions never stopped and were irritating?
items.explanation: Incessant means unceasing and often annoying, matching "drove everyone crazy." Frequent and regular describe repetition neutrally, without the sense of never letting up.

wrong.a: Frequent means often, but it doesn't carry the annoyance or nonstop feeling.
wrong.c: Regular suggests a predictable schedule, not a nonstop stream.
wrong.d: Curious describes the brother's motive, not how constant the questions were.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what incessant means.

chunks.text: The incessant chirping of crickets
continued all night long,
keeping the campers awake until sunrise.
stopping after just a few seconds.

items.hint: Incessant sounds don't stop.
items.explanation: Chirping all night long that keeps campers awake never lets up, which is incessant. Stopping after a few seconds is the opposite.

wrong.c4: Something that stops after a few seconds isn't incessant.

items.prompt: In- means "not," and cess comes from a Latin root meaning "cease" or "stop." What does incessant literally mean?
items.hint: Combine not + stop.
items.explanation: In- (not) + cess (stop) = not stopping. That is why incessant describes something that continues without a break.

wrong.b: The root means stop, not start.
wrong.c: The word parts say nothing about volume.
wrong.d: This ignores in-, which means not.

words.definition: existing in a person or animal from birth rather than learned

hero.text: Bolt's speed was innate; he could outrun the other kids before he ever trained.

words.everyday: Baby sea turtles have an innate drive to crawl toward the ocean as soon as they hatch.

contrast.nonExample: After three years of lessons, Rosa learned to read music.
contrast.explanation: Reading music is a learned skill that took years. Innate abilities are present from birth.

items.prompt: What does "innate" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Newborn babies have an innate ability to grasp a finger placed in their palm.
items.hint: Newborns haven't had time to learn anything yet.
items.explanation: Newborns can grasp without being taught, so the ability is present from birth. That is innate.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Spiders are never taught how to weave webs; even one raised alone in a lab will build a perfect web on its first try. Web-building is ___ behavior.
items.clue: never taught; raised alone; first try
items.hint: If no one teaches it, where does the skill come from?
items.explanation: A spider raised alone builds a web on its first try without being taught. The behavior is innate, present from birth. Learned is the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the passage?
items.passage: Kenji wasn't born a strong writer. His skill was ___ through years of reading, journaling, and revising.
items.clue: wasn't born; years of reading, journaling, and revising
items.hint: The passage says his skill did NOT come from birth.
items.explanation: Kenji's skill came from years of practice, so it was developed, the opposite of innate. Innate, inherited, and instinctive all suggest abilities you're born with.

wrong.a: Innate means present from birth, which the passage denies.
wrong.b: Inherited suggests it came from his parents at birth.
wrong.c: Instinctive means natural and unlearned.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what innate means.

chunks.text: Many scientists believe
humans have an innate ability to learn language,
since babies everywhere start babbling without lessons.
since adults must take classes to gain it.

items.hint: Innate abilities don't need to be taught.
items.explanation: Babies babbling without lessons is evidence of an ability present from birth, which is innate. Needing classes would mean it is learned.

wrong.c4: If it must be gained through classes, it's learned, not innate.

items.prompt: Is this behavior innate?
items.passage: A dog sits when its owner says "sit" after weeks of training with treats.
items.hint: Was the dog born knowing this, or was it taught?
items.explanation: The dog learned to sit through weeks of training, so the behavior is learned, not innate. Innate behaviors need no teaching.

words.definition: to put something at risk of being harmed or lost

hero.text: Rex knew that rushing in alone would jeopardize the whole rescue, so he waited for backup.

words.everyday: Skipping practice before the final could jeopardize the team's chances of winning the championship.

contrast.nonExample: Wearing a helmet protects cyclists from head injuries.
contrast.explanation: A helmet reduces risk. To jeopardize something is to increase the risk of losing or harming it.

items.prompt: What does "jeopardize" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Cheating on the exam could jeopardize Mia's chance of getting into the honors program.
items.hint: What might happen to her chance if she gets caught?
items.explanation: Cheating could make her lose her chance, so it puts her chance at risk. That is jeopardize. Guarantee and improve are the opposite.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Scientists warn that warming oceans could ___ coral reefs. As water heats up, corals lose the algae they depend on and can die.
items.clue: corals lose the algae they depend on and can die
items.hint: Warming water puts the reefs in danger.
items.explanation: Warming water can make corals die, so it puts the reefs at risk. That is jeopardize. Protect is the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "jeopardize" in this sentence?
items.passage: A single careless post online can jeopardize a person's reputation.
items.hint: Jeopardize means putting at risk, not necessarily ruining completely.
items.explanation: Endanger means put at risk, the same as jeopardize. Destroy is too strong: jeopardizing creates a risk of harm, while destroying means the harm already happened.

wrong.a: Destroy means the damage is done; jeopardize only means putting it at risk.
wrong.c: Build is the opposite.
wrong.d: Reveal means show, which isn't about risk.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what jeopardize means.

chunks.text: Building homes on the wetland
would jeopardize
the rare frogs that breed there.
the frogs by giving them more safe places to breed.

items.hint: Jeopardize means putting something in danger.
items.explanation: Building on the frogs' breeding ground puts them at risk, so it would jeopardize them. Giving them more safe places would help them, not jeopardize them.

wrong.c4: Giving frogs safe places protects them, which contradicts jeopardize.

items.prompt: What is the coach worried about?
items.passage: "I know you want to play in the final," the coach told Sami, "but if you play on that sprained ankle, you could jeopardize your whole season."

options.text: Playing could cause Sami to lose the rest of the season.
Sami will definitely score in the final.
Sami's ankle will heal faster if he plays.
The final game has been canceled.

items.clue: on that sprained ankle; your whole season
items.hint: What is at risk if Sami plays injured?
items.explanation: Playing on a sprained ankle risks a worse injury that could end his season. To jeopardize the season is to put it at risk of being lost.

words.definition: slow, sleepy, and lacking energy

hero.text: After three sleepless nights on patrol, Kai felt lethargic and could barely lift off the ground.

words.everyday: The heat wave left everyone lethargic, and even the dogs lay motionless in the shade.

contrast.nonExample: The puppy raced around the yard, chasing every leaf that moved.
contrast.explanation: The puppy is full of energy. Lethargic means sluggish and lacking energy.

items.prompt: Is this person lethargic?
items.passage: After staying up until 3 a.m., Liam dragged himself to school, yawned through every class, and could barely keep his eyes open.
items.hint: Does Liam have energy, or is he sluggish?
items.explanation: Dragging himself, yawning, and barely keeping his eyes open show Liam is slow and lacking energy. That is lethargic.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: In cold weather, lizards become ___ because their bodies depend on outside heat. They move slowly and may barely respond when touched.
items.clue: move slowly; barely respond
items.hint: How would you describe an animal that moves slowly and barely reacts?
items.explanation: Moving slowly and barely responding show a lack of energy. That is lethargic. Aggressive and playful describe active animals.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the passage?
items.passage: Ana wasn't sleepy or worn out. She had plenty of energy; she just didn't feel like cleaning her room. She was ___, not lethargic.
items.clue: plenty of energy; just didn't feel like
items.hint: Lethargic is about low energy. Ana's problem is about desire, not energy.
items.explanation: Ana has energy but no desire to clean, so she is unmotivated. Lethargic, exhausted, drowsy, and sluggish all describe a lack of physical energy, which the passage says she has.

wrong.a: Exhausted means worn out, but Ana has plenty of energy.
wrong.b: Drowsy means sleepy, which the passage rules out.
wrong.d: Sluggish is a synonym for lethargic, which the passage says she isn't.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what lethargic means.

chunks.text: The flu left Grandpa lethargic,
so he spent the week
dozing in his armchair.
running laps around the block.

items.hint: Lethargic people have little energy.
items.explanation: Dozing all week shows Grandpa had no energy, which is lethargic. Running laps would show lots of energy.

wrong.c4: Running laps takes energy, the opposite of lethargic.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the orchestra's performance?
items.passage: The critic wrote that the usually lively orchestra played the dance music at a crawl. The tempos dragged, the rhythms lacked spark, and even the drummer seemed half asleep.
items.clue: at a crawl; tempos dragged; half asleep
items.hint: Look at how slow and sleepy the music sounded.
items.explanation: "At a crawl," "tempos dragged," and "half asleep" describe a slow performance lacking energy. That is lethargic. Energetic is the opposite.

words.definition: to make something bad less severe, harmful, or painful

hero.text: Juniper couldn't stop the wildfire, but she mitigated the damage by clearing a firebreak around the town.

words.everyday: Planting trees along city streets can mitigate summer heat by providing shade.

contrast.nonExample: Leaving the windows open during the storm let rain soak the carpet.
contrast.explanation: Leaving windows open made the damage worse. To mitigate is to reduce how bad something is.

items.prompt: What does "mitigate" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Sandbags along the riverbank helped mitigate the flooding, so only a few basements got wet.
items.hint: Only a few basements got wet. What did the sandbags do to the flooding?
items.explanation: The sandbags made the flooding less severe, so only a few basements got wet. Mitigate means lessen how bad something is.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Earthquakes can't be prevented, but engineers can ___ their effects. Buildings with flexible frames and shock absorbers sway instead of collapsing.
items.clue: can't be prevented, but; sway instead of collapsing
items.hint: Engineers can't stop earthquakes, but they can reduce the harm.
items.explanation: Flexible frames don't stop earthquakes, but they reduce damage. That is mitigating the effects. Mitigating means making something less severe, not preventing it entirely.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the passage?
items.passage: The new vaccine doesn't ___ the disease completely, but it does mitigate the symptoms, turning a dangerous illness into a mild one.
items.clue: doesn't ___ completely, but it does mitigate
items.hint: The sentence contrasts the blank with mitigate. Which word means removing something entirely?
items.explanation: Eliminate means remove completely, which contrasts with mitigate (make less severe). Ease, soften, and reduce all mean about the same as mitigate, so they don't create the contrast the sentence needs.

wrong.a: Ease is a synonym of mitigate, so the contrast wouldn't make sense.
wrong.b: Soften means making something less harsh, close to mitigate.
wrong.c: Reduce is a near-synonym of mitigate.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what mitigate means.

chunks.text: To mitigate the effects of the drought,
the town limited lawn watering
and repaired leaking pipes.
and filled every swimming pool to the top.

items.hint: Mitigating a drought means saving water.
items.explanation: Limiting watering and fixing leaks save water, which lessens the drought's harm. Filling every pool would waste water and make it worse.

wrong.c4: Filling pools wastes water, which would worsen the drought instead of mitigating it.

items.prompt: Is this an example of mitigating a problem?
items.passage: When the factory's smoke started bothering neighbors, owners built a taller smokestack so the fumes blew straight over the town toward a nearby school.
items.hint: Did the harm actually get smaller, or did it just move?
items.explanation: The smoke still harms people; it just moved toward a school. Mitigating means reducing the harm, not shifting it to someone else.

words.definition: a small, subtle difference in meaning, feeling, color, or sound

hero.text: Pixel's voice analyzer could detect every nuance of tone, telling a nervous laugh from a real one.

words.everyday: A good actor captures the nuances of a character, showing that a villain can also be lonely.

contrast.nonExample: The sign said STOP in huge red letters.
contrast.explanation: A huge STOP sign is blunt and obvious. A nuance is a subtle shade of difference that takes care to notice.

items.prompt: What does "nuance" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The singer added a nuance of sadness to the cheerful song by softening her voice on the last line.
items.hint: She only softened her voice slightly. Was the change big or small?
items.explanation: Softening her voice added a small, subtle touch of sadness. A nuance is a subtle shade of feeling or meaning.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Translating poetry is difficult because every ___ matters. A word that means "sad" in one language might also hint at longing or homesickness that has no exact match in another.
items.clue: might also hint at longing or homesickness
items.hint: The passage is about subtle extra meanings in words.
items.explanation: The hint of longing or homesickness is a subtle shade of meaning. That is a nuance, which is why translation is so hard.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the student's essay?
items.passage: Instead of calling the explorer a hero or a villain, Alana's essay showed how he was brave and curious but also caused real harm to the people he met.
items.clue: Instead of calling him a hero or a villain; brave and curious but also caused real harm
items.hint: Complicated can mean confusing. Which word praises her careful attention to shades of meaning?
items.explanation: Nuanced (the adjective form of nuance) means showing subtle differences rather than a simple yes-or-no view. Complicated often suggests confusing, which isn't the praise intended here. Simplistic and biased are the opposite of her approach.

wrong.a: Biased means one-sided, but Alana showed both sides.
wrong.b: Simplistic means too simple, the opposite of her essay.
wrong.d: Complicated can suggest confusing or messy, rather than thoughtfully subtle.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what nuance means.

chunks.text: A skilled painter notices the nuances
between dozens of slightly different blues
in a single evening sky.
by painting everything one flat color.

items.hint: Nuances are tiny differences.
items.explanation: Slightly different blues are small, subtle differences, which are nuances. Painting everything one flat color ignores nuance entirely.

wrong.c4: One flat color has no subtle differences, so it ignores nuance.

items.prompt: What does the music teacher want the band to pay attention to?
items.passage: "You're playing all the right notes," Ms. Ortiz told the band, "but you're missing the nuance. Notice how the melody should swell slightly here and grow just a little quieter there."
items.clue: swell slightly; just a little quieter
items.hint: Look at the words "slightly" and "just a little."
items.explanation: "Swell slightly" and "just a little quieter" describe small, subtle changes. That is what nuance means. Playing louder overall is a big, uniform change.

words.definition: giving the feeling that something bad or harmful is about to happen

hero.text: An ominous silence fell over the city just before the lights went out, and Nova braced herself.

words.everyday: Ominous green clouds gathered on the horizon, and the farmers hurried their animals into the barn.

contrast.nonExample: The morning sky was clear and blue, with a gentle breeze.
contrast.explanation: A clear, calm sky suggests nothing bad. Ominous means seeming to warn of something bad ahead.

items.prompt: Is this situation ominous?
items.passage: As Lena hiked deeper into the woods, the birds suddenly stopped singing, and a low growl came from the bushes.
items.hint: Does this feel like a warning that something bad is coming?
items.explanation: Birds going silent and a low growl suggest danger ahead. That feeling of threat is ominous.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: In the film, the music changes from a bright melody to slow, low notes as the girl opens the attic door. The ___ soundtrack tells viewers something terrible is waiting inside.
items.clue: slow, low notes; something terrible is waiting
items.hint: The music warns viewers that something bad is coming.
items.explanation: Slow, low notes that signal "something terrible is waiting" create a threatening feeling. That is ominous. Cheerful and soothing are the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the passage?
items.passage: The doctor's face was ___: she looked down at the chart for a long time, took a deep breath, and asked the family to sit down before she spoke.
items.clue: looked down for a long time; asked the family to sit down
items.hint: Her behavior signals that bad news may be coming. Scary is close but too casual.
items.explanation: Ominous means suggesting that something bad is coming, which fits signs of bad news. Scary is more casual and suggests fright, not quiet warning. Nothing suggests the doctor is angry.

wrong.a: Scary is casual and suggests something frightening, not a quiet warning sign.
wrong.b: Her behavior suggests bad news, not good.
wrong.c: She seems serious, not angry.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what ominous means.

chunks.text: The ship's captain grew worried
when an ominous rumble
rose from deep inside the engine room.
promised a calm and pleasant voyage.

items.hint: Ominous sounds warn of trouble.
items.explanation: A rumble from the engine room that worries the captain hints at danger, so it is ominous. Something ominous can't promise a pleasant voyage.

wrong.c4: An ominous sign warns of trouble; it can't promise something pleasant.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly OPPOSITE to "ominous" in this sentence?
items.passage: The first reports from the rescue team were ominous.
items.hint: Ominous makes you fear the worst. What makes you feel better?
items.explanation: Reassuring means making people feel things will be okay, the opposite of ominous. Menacing is a synonym.

wrong.a: Menacing is close in meaning to ominous.
wrong.b: Length has nothing to do with hope or threat.
wrong.d: Urgent reports could be good or bad news.

words.definition: a statement or situation that seems to contradict itself but may still be true

hero.text: Bolt laughed at the paradox: the faster he rushed, the longer the repair took.

words.everyday: It's a paradox that having too many choices at a store can make it harder to pick anything.

contrast.nonExample: The more you practice piano, the better you get.
contrast.explanation: That makes perfect sense; nothing contradicts. A paradox seems impossible or contradictory at first but holds some truth.

items.prompt: Which statement is a paradox?

options.text: "I must be cruel to be kind."

items.hint: Look for a statement that seems to contradict itself but might make sense.
items.explanation: Being cruel and kind seem like opposites, yet sometimes a hard truth helps someone. That seeming contradiction is a paradox.

wrong.a: This is a plain scientific fact, with no contradiction.
wrong.c: This is an opinion, not a contradiction.
wrong.d: This is a simple statement about the calendar.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Rachel noticed a strange ___: the more she tried to fall asleep, the more awake she felt. Only when she stopped trying did sleep finally come.
items.clue: the more she tried, the more awake she felt
items.hint: Trying harder had the opposite effect. What is that kind of contradiction called?
items.explanation: Trying to sleep made her more awake, which seems contradictory but was true. That is a paradox.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the passage?
items.passage: Leo forgot his umbrella on the one day it rained all week. That was just bad luck, a ___, not a true paradox, since nothing about it contradicts itself.
items.clue: just bad luck; nothing about it contradicts itself
items.hint: The passage says the event is NOT a contradiction. It is chance.
items.explanation: A coincidence is two things happening together by chance. A paradox involves a seeming contradiction, which the passage says isn't present. Contradiction, puzzle, and riddle all suggest something that seems impossible or confusing.

wrong.b: A puzzle suggests something to figure out, but this is just bad luck.
wrong.c: The passage says nothing contradicts itself.
wrong.d: A riddle is a word game, not bad luck.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what paradox means.

chunks.text: It is a paradox
that the loneliest people
can sometimes be found in the busiest cities.
usually live alone far from other people.

items.hint: A paradox seems contradictory. Which ending surprises you?
items.explanation: Feeling lonely surrounded by millions of people seems contradictory, yet it happens. That is a paradox. Lonely people living alone far away makes sense, so there's no contradiction.

wrong.c4: Lonely people living far away is expected; there's no contradiction, so it isn't a paradox.

items.prompt: Does this describe a paradox?
items.passage: A famous saying goes: "The more you learn, the more you realize how little you know."
items.hint: Learning more should make you feel you know more. Does the saying say that?
items.explanation: Learning more and feeling you know less seems contradictory, yet many people find it true. That makes the saying a paradox.

words.definition: lasting forever or continuing for a very long time without stopping

hero.text: Kai dreamed of building a perpetual energy source that would power the academy forever.

words.everyday: Near the North Pole in summer, the sun never sets, creating a period of perpetual daylight.

contrast.nonExample: The fireworks show lasted twenty minutes.
contrast.explanation: Twenty minutes has a clear end. Perpetual means going on forever or without stopping.

items.prompt: What does "perpetual" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The deep ocean floor exists in perpetual darkness; sunlight never reaches it.
items.hint: "Sunlight never reaches it." Does the darkness ever stop?
items.explanation: Since sunlight never reaches it, the darkness never ends. Perpetual means never-ending or continuing without stopping.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: For centuries, inventors dreamed of machines with ___ motion: machines that would run forever without any fuel. Scientists now know the laws of physics make it impossible.
items.clue: run forever without any fuel
items.hint: The machine was supposed to run forever.
items.explanation: A machine that runs "forever" without fuel would have perpetual motion. Temporary means the opposite: lasting a short time.

items.prompt: Which word best captures the exaggeration in this sentence?
items.passage: "My brother is in a state of ___ hunger," Ines joked. "He finishes dinner and asks for a snack five minutes later."
items.clue: Ines joked; five minutes later
items.hint: Ines is exaggerating that the hunger never ends.
items.explanation: Perpetual means never-ending, and here it's used as a playful exaggeration: her brother's hunger seems to never stop. Occasional, slight, and brief all suggest the hunger is small or rare.

wrong.a: Occasional means now and then, which doesn't match the joke.
wrong.b: Slight means small, but the joke is about how constant it is.
wrong.d: Brief means short-lived, the opposite of the exaggeration.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what perpetual means.

chunks.text: The mountain's peak is covered
in perpetual snow
that never melts, even in midsummer.
that melts away completely every spring.

items.hint: Perpetual things never stop or go away.
items.explanation: Snow that never melts, even in summer, lasts forever, so it is perpetual. Snow that melts every spring is seasonal, not perpetual.

wrong.c4: Snow that melts every spring comes and goes, so it isn't perpetual.

items.prompt: What does the passage suggest about the river town?
items.passage: Living beside the waterfall, the villagers were surrounded by a perpetual roar. Children born there grew up never knowing true silence.

options.text: The noise only happened during storms.

items.clue: never knowing true silence
items.hint: If children never knew silence, how long did the roar last?
items.explanation: "Never knowing true silence" shows the roar never stopped. That is what perpetual means.

words.definition: very deep, great, or intense in meaning, feeling, or effect

hero.text: Meeting the retired hero who had trained her grandmother had a profound effect on Nova; she decided to dedicate her life to teaching.

words.everyday: The invention of the printing press had a profound impact on education, making books available to ordinary people.

contrast.nonExample: Changing the color of the classroom's pencil cup made no real difference.
contrast.explanation: A tiny change with little effect is trivial. Profound describes something with a deep, lasting impact or meaning.

items.prompt: What does "profound" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: Losing her grandmother caused Ellie profound sadness that lasted for many months.
items.hint: The sadness lasted for many months. Was it small or deep?
items.explanation: Sadness that lasts many months is intense and deep. Profound means very deep or great. Mild is the opposite.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The effect of penicillin on medicine was ___. Infections that once killed millions could suddenly be cured in days.
items.clue: once killed millions; cured in days
items.hint: How big was the change to medicine?
items.explanation: Going from killing millions to cured in days is a huge, deep change. That is a profound effect. Minor is the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word is most nearly OPPOSITE to "profound" in this sentence?
items.passage: The old philosopher was known for asking profound questions about the meaning of life.
items.hint: Profound means deep. What means only on the surface?
items.explanation: Superficial means shallow, only on the surface, the opposite of profound. Serious and difficult questions could also be profound, so they aren't opposites.

wrong.a: Serious questions can be profound; this isn't an opposite.
wrong.b: Difficult questions are often profound.
wrong.d: Ancient refers to age, not depth.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what profound means.

chunks.text: Reading the diary of a girl in wartime
had a profound effect on Marcus,
changing how he thought about courage forever.
which he forgot about by lunchtime.

items.hint: A profound effect is deep and lasting.
items.explanation: Changing how he thought about courage forever is a deep, lasting effect, so it is profound. Something forgotten by lunchtime had no profound effect.

wrong.c4: If he forgot it by lunch, the effect wasn't deep or lasting, so it wasn't profound.

items.prompt: Which word best describes the speaker's insight?
items.passage: At the graduation, the speaker said, "You will forget most of the facts you learned here, but you will never forget how it felt to be believed in." The audience sat silent, thinking about it long after she finished.
items.clue: The audience sat silent, thinking about it long after
items.hint: Clever is quick and witty. Which word suggests deep meaning that makes people reflect?
items.explanation: Profound means deep in meaning, and the audience's long, silent reflection shows the insight affected them deeply. Clever suggests witty or smart but not necessarily deep. Complex means having many parts, but her statement was simple.

wrong.a: Clever suggests wit, not depth that makes people reflect.
wrong.c: Complex means complicated, but her words were simple.
wrong.d: Nothing suggests the audience laughed.

words.definition: showing good judgment and care in planning for the future or avoiding risks

hero.text: Before flying into the storm, Juniper made the prudent choice to check her equipment and tell the team her route.

words.everyday: It's prudent to save part of every paycheck in case of an emergency.

contrast.nonExample: Tyler spent all his savings on concert tickets the day before rent was due.
contrast.explanation: Ignoring an upcoming need is careless. Prudent people think ahead and avoid unnecessary risks.

items.prompt: Which choice is prudent?

options.text: Hiking a mountain trail without water or a map
Checking the weather and packing a raincoat before a long hike
Racing down the trail in the dark
Leaving the trail to take a shortcut over a cliff

items.hint: Which hiker plans ahead and avoids risk?
items.explanation: Checking the weather and packing a raincoat show good judgment and planning. That is prudent.

wrong.a: Going without water or a map is risky.
wrong.c: Racing in the dark is reckless.
wrong.d: A shortcut over a cliff is dangerous, not wise.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: With forecasters predicting a powerful hurricane, the ___ store owner boarded up her windows and moved her stock to higher ground two days early.
items.clue: boarded up her windows; two days early
items.hint: She prepared early to avoid damage.
items.explanation: Boarding up windows and moving stock early shows good judgment and planning. That is prudent. Careless and reckless describe the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the passage's tone?
items.passage: Some called the senator's refusal to spend any money at all ___. Even when the bridge was crumbling, he would not approve repairs.
items.clue: refusal to spend any money at all; even when the bridge was crumbling
items.hint: Prudent is a compliment. Is the writer praising him?
items.explanation: Stingy means unwilling to spend, even when spending is needed, a negative judgment. Prudent, wise, and sensible all praise good judgment, but refusing to fix a crumbling bridge isn't good judgment.

wrong.a: Prudent is praise; refusing to fix a crumbling bridge is not careful judgment.
wrong.c: Wise is positive, but the passage criticizes him.
wrong.d: Sensible is positive and doesn't fit ignoring a crumbling bridge.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what prudent means.

chunks.text: It would be prudent
to back up your essay
in case your computer crashes.
by deleting every saved copy.

items.hint: Prudent means planning ahead to avoid problems.
items.explanation: Backing up an essay in case of a crash is wise planning, which is prudent. Deleting every copy would invite disaster.

wrong.c4: Deleting every copy is the opposite of careful planning.

items.prompt: Which line uses "prudent" naturally?

options.text: "It was prudent of me to skip studying; the test was easy anyway."
"The prudent puppy chewed up all the shoes."
"Let's be prudent and dive into the lake without checking how deep it is."
"Since the ice is thin, it's prudent to stay off the pond."

items.hint: Prudent describes a careful choice that avoids risk.
items.explanation: Staying off thin ice is a careful decision that avoids danger, so prudent fits. Diving without checking depth and skipping studying are risky, not prudent.

wrong.a: Skipping studying was lucky, not prudent; prudence is about careful planning.
wrong.b: Chewing shoes shows no good judgment.
wrong.c: Diving without checking depth is reckless.

words.definition: refusing to give up or let go; very determined and persistent

hero.text: Rex was tenacious: he searched the collapsed tunnel for twelve hours until he found the missing hiker.

words.everyday: The tenacious reporter called sources for months until she uncovered the truth about the polluted river.

contrast.nonExample: After one failed attempt at the puzzle, Ava tossed it aside and never tried again.
contrast.explanation: Giving up after one try is the opposite of tenacious. Tenacious people keep going despite setbacks.

items.prompt: Is this person tenacious?
items.passage: Wilma Rudolph was told as a child she might never walk normally. She did exercises every day for years and later won three Olympic gold medals in running.
items.hint: Did she give up, or keep going despite the odds?
items.explanation: Doing exercises every day for years despite a discouraging prediction shows she refused to give up. That is tenacious.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: Ivy plants are ___ climbers. Their tiny roots grip brick and stone so tightly that pulling them off can damage the wall itself.
items.clue: grip so tightly; pulling them off can damage the wall
items.hint: The ivy holds on and won't let go.
items.explanation: Roots that grip so tightly they damage walls when removed won't let go. Tenacious can mean holding on firmly, as here, or refusing to give up.

items.prompt: Which word best fits the passage's admiring tone?
items.passage: The scientist tested more than 1,000 materials before finding one that worked. Her colleagues admired how ___ she was in the face of constant failure.
items.clue: admired; in the face of constant failure
items.hint: Stubborn and obsessed both mean not stopping, but they sound critical.
items.explanation: Tenacious means persistent in an admirable way, which fits colleagues who "admired" her. Stubborn and obsessed suggest unreasonable or unhealthy persistence. Lucky ignores her hard work.

wrong.a: Stubborn suggests unreasonable refusal to change, a negative tone.
wrong.b: Obsessed suggests unhealthy focus, not admirable persistence.
wrong.d: Lucky ignores the 1,000 tests; her success came from effort.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what tenacious means.

chunks.text: The tenacious goalie
kept diving for every shot
even though her team was losing badly.
until she got tired and stopped trying.

items.hint: Tenacious people don't give up, even when things look bad.
items.explanation: Diving for every shot while losing badly shows refusal to give up, which is tenacious. Stopping when tired is the opposite.

wrong.c4: Giving up when tired contradicts tenacious.

items.prompt: Tenacious comes from the Latin tenere, "to hold." Which other word shares this root and a related meaning?
items.hint: Look for a word that means holding on to something.
items.explanation: Retain means to hold on to or keep, from the same root as tenacious. A tenacious person holds on and won't let go. Tennis, tender, and tent only look similar.

wrong.a: Tennis looks similar but has no connection to holding.
wrong.b: Tender means gentle or soft, unrelated to holding on.
wrong.d: Tent comes from a root meaning stretch, not hold.

words.definition: likely to change suddenly and unpredictably, often for the worse

hero.text: The situation at the protest was volatile, so Kai kept calm and helped people move to safety before it could explode.

words.everyday: Mountain weather is volatile; a sunny morning can turn into a dangerous storm within an hour.

contrast.nonExample: The temperature in the cave stays at 12 degrees Celsius all year.
contrast.explanation: Something that never changes is stable. Volatile means likely to change suddenly and unpredictably.

items.prompt: What does "volatile" mean in this sentence?
items.passage: The price of the new video game was volatile, jumping from $20 to $60 and back again in a single week.
items.hint: Look at what the price did in one week.
items.explanation: The price jumped up and down quickly and unpredictably. That is volatile. Fixed means the opposite.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The two countries had been close to war for months, and a single insult at the meeting could have set off fighting. Diplomats described the situation as extremely ___.
items.clue: close to war; a single insult could have set off fighting
items.hint: One small spark could make things explode.
items.explanation: If a single insult could start a war, the situation could change suddenly for the worse. That is volatile. Peaceful and settled are the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word best describes Coach Briggs?
items.passage: Coach Briggs could be laughing one moment and screaming the next. Players never knew what might set him off.
items.clue: laughing one moment and screaming the next; never knew what might set him off
items.hint: Angry describes one mood. Which word describes moods that swing suddenly?
items.explanation: Volatile describes someone whose mood changes suddenly and unpredictably. Angry is a single mood, and strict means firm with rules. Neither captures the sudden swings.

wrong.a: Strict is about firm rules, not unpredictable moods.
wrong.c: Angry describes one feeling, but he also laughs; the key is the sudden change.
wrong.d: Energetic means lively, not unpredictable.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what volatile means.

chunks.text: Because the stock market was volatile,
investors watched nervously
as prices swung wildly each hour.
as prices stayed exactly the same all year.

items.hint: Volatile means changing suddenly and unpredictably.
items.explanation: Prices swinging wildly each hour show sudden, unpredictable change, which is volatile. Prices staying the same all year would be stable.

wrong.c4: Prices that never change are stable, not volatile.

items.prompt: Why does the chemistry teacher store the liquid so carefully?
items.passage: The chemistry teacher keeps that liquid in a sealed metal cabinet, far from any heat or sparks. "It's highly volatile," she explains. "A small change in temperature could make it react violently."

options.text: It is unstable and could react suddenly.

items.clue: a small change in temperature could make it react violently
items.hint: What could a small change in temperature cause?
items.explanation: "A small change could make it react violently" shows the liquid is unstable and could change suddenly. In science, volatile also describes substances that evaporate or react easily.

words.definition: more than is needed; unnecessary or extra

hero.text: Pixel removed the superfluous buttons from her gadget, keeping only the three she actually used.

words.everyday: The editor cut superfluous words from the article, turning a 900-word draft into a sharp 500-word story.

contrast.nonExample: A recipe for bread needs flour, water, yeast, and salt.
contrast.explanation: Each ingredient is necessary. Superfluous things are extra and could be removed without any loss.

items.prompt: Is the item superfluous?
items.passage: Mateo packed five flashlights for a one-night camping trip, even though one was plenty.
items.hint: Did Mateo pack more than he needed?
items.explanation: One flashlight was plenty, so the other four were extra and unnecessary. That makes them superfluous.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the passage.
items.passage: The speech was meant to last five minutes, but the speaker kept repeating the same points and adding long stories that had nothing to do with the topic. Most of it was ___.
items.clue: repeating the same points; nothing to do with the topic
items.hint: Repeated points and off-topic stories are not needed.
items.explanation: Repeating points and adding unrelated stories made much of the speech unnecessary. That is superfluous. Essential and focused are the opposite.

items.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to "superfluous" in this sentence?
items.passage: The teacher said the decorative borders on the lab report were superfluous; only the data mattered.
items.hint: "Only the data mattered." What does that say about the borders?
items.explanation: Since only the data mattered, the borders were not needed. Unnecessary matches superfluous. The borders might be beautiful, but that isn't what superfluous means.

wrong.a: The borders may be pretty, but superfluous means not needed, not attractive.
wrong.c: Nothing suggests the borders were messy.
wrong.d: Required is the opposite.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows what superfluous means.

chunks.text: Since the room was already bright,
turning on a fourth lamp
seemed superfluous.
was absolutely necessary to see anything.

items.hint: Superfluous means extra, more than needed.
items.explanation: In an already bright room, a fourth lamp isn't needed, so it is superfluous. If it were necessary to see, it wouldn't be superfluous.

wrong.c4: If the lamp was necessary, it wasn't superfluous; and the room was already bright.

items.prompt: Which word best completes the editor's note?
items.passage: "Your sentence 'He nodded his head yes in agreement' has ___ words," the editor wrote. "Nodding already means yes and agreement. Just write 'He nodded.'"
items.clue: Nodding already means yes and agreement
items.hint: The editor wants to cut words that repeat what's already said.
items.explanation: "His head," "yes," and "in agreement" repeat what nodding already means, so they are extra. Superfluous fits. Missing is the opposite problem.

wrong.b: Nothing is missing; there are too many words.
wrong.c: The words are spelled correctly; they're just unnecessary.
wrong.d: The editor is criticizing the extra words, not praising them.
